seo.title: HTS Chapter 10: Cereals — Tariff Rates & Import Duties | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 66 HTS Chapter 10 tariff lines: wheat, rye, barley, oats, corn, rice (jasmine, basmati, parboiled), grain sorghum, quinoa, millet and wild rice. General, FTA and Column 2 rates, filterable by product name.

overview.intro:
Chapter 10 covers cereal grains: wheat, rye, barley, oats, corn, rice, grain sorghum, buckwheat, millet, quinoa and wild rice. Its **66 tariff lines** carry small printed rates: 0.35¢/kg on most wheat, 1.4¢/kg on milled rice, Free on oats and rye. The one large percentage is **11.2% on parboiled rice**.

The printed rate is rarely what decides the cost. The U.S. imported $3.17B of cereals in 2025: $1.64B of it rice, mostly jasmine from Thailand and basmati from India, and $1.25B from Canada, mostly wheat and oats. USMCA-qualifying grain from Canada and Mexico enters free. Grain from elsewhere pays the base rate **plus an extra duty by country**: since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff on 60 economies adds 12.5% for Thailand and Vietnam and 10% for India and Pakistan, sets 10% in total for the EU, and China and Brazil pay up to 37.5% (see Rates by country). Seed for sowing and a few other lines are exempt from that 60-economy tariff.

workedExamples.title: 20 tonnes of jasmine rice from Thailand
workedExamples.body: Milled jasmine rice is 1.4¢/kg: 20,000 kg × $0.014 = **$280** base duty. Thailand is one of the 60 economies in the 2026 Section 301 action, so 12.5% of the shipment's value is added (9903.05.77). At $1,000 a tonne that is $20,000 × 12.5% = **$2,500**, or **$2,780** in all. The extra duty is about 90% of the bill.

workedExamples.title: $50,000 of quinoa from Peru or Bolivia
workedExamples.body: The general rate is 1.1% ($550). A Peru TPA claim (SPI **PE**) makes the base rate Free, but the 12.5% Section 301 duty on Peruvian goods (9903.05.63) still applies with an FTA claim (U.S. note 52(a)): **$6,250**. Bolivia is not one of the 60 economies and has no FTA with the U.S., so Bolivian quinoa pays only the 1.1% base rate: **$550**.

workedExamples.title: A 90-tonne railcar of Canadian milling wheat
workedExamples.body: The general rate is 0.35¢/kg. With a USMCA claim (SPI **S**) the base rate is Free and the 10% Section 301 duty on Canadian goods does not apply (9903.05.93): **$0**. Wheat that does not qualify pays 90,000 kg × $0.0035 = $315 plus 10% of its value (9903.05.29); at $280 a tonne that is $2,520, or **$2,835** in all.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** (a) The products specified in the headings of this chapter are to be classified in those headings only if grains are present, whether or not in the ear or on the stalk. (b) This chapter does not cover grains which have been hulled or otherwise worked. However, rice, husked, milled, polished, glazed, parboiled, or broken remains classified in heading 1006. Similarly, quinoa from which the pericarp has been wholly or partly removed in order to separate the saponin, but which has not undergone any other processes, remains classified in heading 1008.

**Note 2.** Heading 1005 does not cover sweet corn (chapter 7).

**Subheading Note 1.** The term "durum wheat" means wheat of the *Triticum durum* species and the hybrids derived from the interspecific crossing of *Triticum durum* which have the same number (28) of chromosomes as that species.
notes.additionalUsNotes:
**Note 1.** In subheading 1005.10, the expression "seed" covers only seed corn or maize which is certified by a responsible officer or agency of a foreign government in accordance with the rules and regulations of that government to have been grown and approved especially for use as seed, in containers marked with the foreign government's official certified seed corn tags.

**Statistical Note 1.** For a list of approved standards for "Certified organic", see General Statistical Note 6.

seo.title: HTS Chapter 10 Cereals Tariff Updates 2025–2026: Rice, Wheat & Grain Duties | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 10 (cereals) since January 2025: base rates on all 66 lines, the end of the IEEPA duties, the 2026 Section 122 surcharge and the Section 301 tariffs on rice, wheat and grain, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). On every one of the 66 Chapter 10 lines the base rates are the same in both.

Everything that changed came on top of the base rate, as extra duties set by country. The 2025 IEEPA duties (Canada +35%, Mexico +25%, the reciprocal tariff on everyone else) **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026**, grain from 60 economies pays a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%**: Thailand and Vietnam +12.5%, India and Pakistan +10%, the EU 10% in total. Seed for sowing, non-malting barley, canary seed, fonio and triticale are on that action's exemption list. China pays more because older Section 301 duties stack on top (**up to 37.5%**), and so does Brazil (**37.5%**). **USMCA-qualifying grain from Canada and Mexico is still exempt.**
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 10 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the China Section 301 Lists 3 and 4A, the scheduled Nicaragua Section 301 tariff, and the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 10 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 66 Chapter 10 tariff lines carry the same General, FTA and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; none changed and none is new or renumbered. Revision 21 changed only Chapter 38 and a China exclusion note in Chapter 99.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duties and import bans do not reach cereals
changes.detail: Proclamations of July 20 and September 8, 2026 put 50% Section 338 duties, and from September 29 import bans, on some Canadian alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motor vehicles. No Chapter 10 line is on the lists in U.S. note 51 (9903.03.12–9903.03.14), so Canadian wheat, oats and barley are not affected.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover cereals
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84), on 51 of the 66 Chapter 10 lines. The exemption list in U.S. note 52(b) (9903.05.86) covers seed for sowing of wheat, rye, barley, oats, corn, sorghum and millet, plus non-malting barley (1003.90.40), canary seed, fonio and triticale. EU goods pay 10% in total and Japan and South Korea 12.5% in total. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94).

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01). The exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03) covers four Chapter 10 subheadings: non-malting barley (1003.90.40), canary seed, fonio and triticale. From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) on Canadian and Mexican grain still apply.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. Four Chapter 10 subheadings were on the product exemption list (9903.03.03): non-malting barley (1003.90.40), canary seed, fonio and triticale. Rice, wheat, oats and corn were not. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: Extra 25% duty on Indian goods removed
changes.detail: Executive Order 14384 ended the additional 25% duty on products of India tied to purchases of Russian oil (9903.01.84–9903.01.89), for goods entered from February 7, 2026. India's reciprocal duty ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 renewed AGOA retroactively from September 30, 2025. AGOA (SPI D) is listed on every dutiable Chapter 10 line, so cereals from AGOA beneficiary countries enter at a Free base rate. GSP (SPI A, A*, A+) remains expired since December 31, 2020.

changes.title: Nicaragua Section 301 tariff scheduled for 2027 and 2028
changes.detail: USTR set a tariff on products of Nicaragua that is 0% until the end of 2026, then +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01). It applies only to goods that do not claim a special rate such as CAFTA-DR. It reaches all 66 Chapter 10 lines; Nicaragua also pays the 12.5% 2026 forced-labor tariff (9903.05.58).

changes.title: Agricultural exemption covered only four Chapter 10 lines
changes.detail: The exemption list for the reciprocal duties (U.S. note 2(v)(iii)(a), heading 9903.01.32), widened for agricultural products from November 13, 2025, included non-malting barley (1003.90.40), canary seed, fonio and triticale. Rice, wheat, oats and corn stayed subject to the reciprocal duties until they ended on February 24, 2026.

changes.detail: Executive Order 14329 added 25% on products of India, on top of the reciprocal duty, because India was importing Russian oil. It covered basmati and other Indian rice. Removed February 7, 2026.

changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of cereals were **$3.17B in 2025**, down 4.5% from $3.33B in 2024 and below the 2023 peak of $3.59B. Two lanes make up most of it.

**Rice ($1.64B, 52%)** comes mostly from Asia: Thailand shipped $966M (up 9.3%), almost all jasmine and other milled rice; India $401M of rice, mainly basmati; Pakistan $50M. Milled rice (1006.30) alone was $1.56B.

**Canada ($1.25B, 39%)** supplies nearly all the wheat ($693M of $707M), oats ($343.8M of $344.1M), barley and rye. Canadian shipments fell 4.8%; U.S. imports of durum wheat (1001.19) dropped from $241M to $188M.

Smaller lanes: corn ($245M) from Canada, Argentina, Chile and Türkiye, of which $75M was seed corn (down from $118M); and quinoa ($109M) from Peru and Bolivia. Rye imports halved, from $92M to $50M.

These are 2025 figures, the latest full year. They were shipped under the 2025 IEEPA duties, which ended in February 2026, and before the Section 301 tariffs that started July 24, 2026.

seo.title: Importing Rice, Wheat & Grain: Required Documents, APHIS & FDA Rules, Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 10) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The permits, certificates and rules for each HTS Chapter 10 line (FDA prior notice and FSVP, USDA APHIS grain and seed rules, Federal Seed Act) and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, FTA claims, seed lines, Chapter 98 and drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
For cereals the paperwork depends on whether the grain is **food or seed**. Grain for food or feed needs FDA prior notice, a registered foreign facility and an importer with a Foreign Supplier Verification Program. Seed for sowing goes through USDA APHIS plant-for-planting rules and the Federal Seed Act instead. Some origins add pest rules: rice from khapra-beetle countries such as India and Pakistan, wheat from Karnal-bunt regions, corn from parts of Asia.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule: claim **USMCA** or another **FTA**, classify genuine **seed for sowing** correctly, use a **Chapter 98** provision when the purpose fits, or claim **drawback** on grain that is exported. Each one depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on grain from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The Section 301 duty (10% of value for Canada or Mexico) plus any base rate, such as 0.35¢/kg on wheat
levers.appliesTo: All 66 lines, for grain that qualifies as originating under USMCA
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer. It need not follow a prescribed format; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: Claiming without a valid certification exposes the entry to the 10% Section 301 duty plus penalties. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Claim an FTA or AGOA rate on the base duty
levers.saves: The base rate: Free instead of up to 11.2% (parboiled rice) or 1.4¢/kg (milled rice). The Section 301 duty for the country still applies.
levers.appliesTo: The 57 dutiable lines, for goods originating in an FTA partner (for example Peru, Chile, Colombia, Australia, South Korea, CAFTA-DR countries) or an AGOA country
levers.document: The origin documentation the agreement requires, with the special program indicator (PE, CL, CO, AU, KR, P, D …) on the entry.
levers.caveat: FTA and AGOA claims do not remove the 2026 Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)); for Peru and Chile the 12.5% still applies. GSP (A, A*, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020, so a GSP claim pays the general rate. AGOA runs through December 31, 2026.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Enter genuine seed for sowing under the seed lines
levers.saves: The 2026 Section 301 duty (10% or 12.5% of value) for most of the 60 economies, because seed lines are on the exemption list; seed corn and seed rye are also Free at base
levers.document: For seed corn, the foreign government's official certified seed corn tags on the containers (Additional U.S. Note 1). For all seed, the APHIS permit or phytosanitary certificate and the Federal Seed Act declaration and labels (see the rules below).
levers.caveat: Only grain that really is seed for sowing qualifies; grain entered as seed and then milled or fed is misclassified. China (List 3 or 4A) and Brazil (25%) still charge their other Section 301 duties on most seed lines.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(b) (9903.05.86)

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision when the purpose fits
levers.saves: The base rate and the 2026 Section 301 duty: each provision below is Free in the schedule
levers.appliesTo: Grain imported for a specific purpose, whatever its Chapter 10 line
levers.document: Evidence of the qualifying purpose: proof of U.S. origin and export for returned goods (19 CFR 10.1), or a bond for samples and test lots.
levers.caveat: The 2026 Section 301 duties (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) do not apply to goods properly entered under a Chapter 98 provision when CBP agrees the entry is appropriate, except entries under 9802.00.40–9802.00.80 (U.S. note 52(a)). The entry must qualify, so get CBP's agreement (or a ruling) before relying on it.

provisions.text: U.S. grain returned after export without being advanced in value or improved in condition, for example a rejected rice or wheat cargo
Samples solely for use in taking orders
Articles solely for testing, experimental or review purposes, for example a grain lot for milling or malting trials

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Claim drawback on grain that is exported
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties, taxes and fees paid on imported grain that is later exported or destroyed, or on substituted grain of the same 8-digit line
levers.appliesTo: Any line, for importers or millers that also export
levers.document: A drawback claim filed electronically with CBP, with import and export records linking the two; for substitution, records showing the exported grain is classifiable under the same 8-digit subheading.
levers.caveat: Drawback has strict time limits (5 years from import) and record-keeping rules. Check with CBP which Chapter 99 duties are refundable for your claim.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: a ruling fixes the classification (seed or grain, parboiled or milled, malting or other barley) before the goods arrive
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the classification decides the rate
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the grain, its processing and its intended use.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a different shipment may need its own.

rules.title: Prior notice of imported food: file before the grain arrives
Food facility registration for foreign mills, warehouses and packers that handle the grain (farms are exempt)
Foreign Supplier Verification Program: the U.S. importer must verify each foreign supplier
Seed and paddy rice for planting: plants-for-planting rules, phytosanitary certificate or APHIS permit, port inspection
Imported agricultural seed: importer's declaration of kind, variety, origin and use, and labels on each container; seed with noxious-weed seeds is refused

Corn, sorghum and millet: corn from southeastern Asia, Australia, New Zealand (except clean seed), Oceania, the Philippines, Japan and nearby areas is prohibited; clean shelled corn and clean sorghum or millet seed enter under the 319.41 conditions

Wheat and triticale from Karnal-bunt regions (Afghanistan, India, Iran, Iraq, Mexico, Nepal, Pakistan, South Africa): only from a recognized free area or tested free, with a phytosanitary certificate carrying the Karnal-bunt declaration

Rice from khapra-beetle countries (including India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Sri Lanka, Egypt, Türkiye): phytosanitary certificate stating the shipment was inspected and found free of khapra beetle; not allowed in passenger baggage

citations.label: APHIS: Countries Infested with Khapra Beetle (06/2022)

rules.title: Paddy (unhusked) rice is restricted as seed under the plants-for-planting rules; rice straw and hulls need a permit and treatment

groups.label: Wheat & meslin
groups.note: Seed wheat (1001.11, 1001.91) follows the APHIS seed and Federal Seed Act rules; milling wheat follows the FDA food rules. Wheat from a Karnal-bunt region needs the Karnal-bunt declaration either way.

groups.label: Rye
groups.note: Seed rye for sowing (1002.10.00.10) follows the seed rules; other rye the FDA food rules.

groups.label: Barley
groups.note: Seed barley (1003.10) follows the seed rules; malting and other barley the FDA food rules.

groups.label: Oats
groups.note: Seed oats (1004.10) follow the seed rules; other oats the FDA food rules.

groups.label: Corn (maize)
groups.note: Seed corn (1005.10) follows the seed rules and needs foreign-government certified seed tags to be classified as seed; other corn and popcorn follow the FDA food rules. Corn from parts of Asia and Oceania is prohibited (7 CFR 319.24).

groups.label: Rice
groups.note: All rice for food follows the FDA rules; rice from khapra-beetle countries such as India and Pakistan also needs the khapra-beetle declaration. Paddy rice (1006.10) is restricted as seed.

groups.label: Grain sorghum
groups.note: Seed sorghum (1007.10) follows the seed rules; grain sorghum the FDA food rules and the 319.41 conditions.

groups.label: Buckwheat, millet, quinoa & other cereals
groups.note: Millet seed (1008.21) follows the seed rules and the 319.41 conditions; quinoa, buckwheat, canary seed and wild rice follow the FDA food rules. Triticale from a Karnal-bunt region needs the Karnal-bunt declaration.

seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people actually search about cereal tariffs: is there a tariff on rice, the tariff on basmati from India and jasmine from Thailand, Canadian wheat and oats, HS codes for rice, wheat, corn and quinoa, and how to import rice.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing cereals into the U.S.: tariffs by country, HS codes and entry requirements. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: USMCA-qualifying grain from Canada and Mexico enters free: no base rate, no extra duty. Canada supplies nearly all U.S. wheat and oats imports.

The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026. Since July 24, 2026 the extra duty is a Section 301 tariff: +12.5% for Thailand and Vietnam, +10% for India and Pakistan, 10% in total for the EU, up to +37.5% for China and Brazil. Seed for sowing is exempt for most countries.

Rice is half the chapter's imports, and for rice the extra duty is now most of the bill: 12.5% of value on Thai jasmine against a 1.4¢/kg base rate. Rice from India and Pakistan also needs a khapra-beetle phytosanitary declaration.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on rice imported into the U.S.?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on rice
faqs.answer: Yes, but the base rate is small: 1.4¢/kg on milled rice (including jasmine and basmati), 0.83¢/kg on brown basmati, 2.1¢/kg on other brown rice, 0.44¢/kg on broken rice and 11.2% on parboiled rice. Since July 24, 2026 rice from 60 economies also pays a Section 301 tariff: +12.5% for Thailand and Vietnam, +10% for India and Pakistan, 10% in total for the EU, and up to +37.5% for China and Brazil. USMCA-qualifying rice from Canada or Mexico is free.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on rice from India (basmati)?
searchedAs: tariff on rice from india to usa
us tariffs on rice from india
is there tariff on indian rice
faqs.answer: Milled basmati (1006.30.90.59) pays 1.4¢/kg and brown basmati (1006.20.20) 0.83¢/kg, plus 10% of value under the 2026 Section 301 tariff on Indian goods (9903.05.44), in effect since July 24, 2026. The 2025 IEEPA duties on India, including the extra 25% tied to Russian oil, ended in February 2026 (February 7 and February 24). Rice from India also needs a phytosanitary certificate stating it was found free of khapra beetle (7 CFR 319.75-2).

faqs.question: What is the tariff on jasmine rice from Thailand?
faqs.answer: Milled jasmine rice (1006.30.90.57) pays 1.4¢/kg plus 12.5% of value under the Section 301 tariff on Thai goods (9903.05.77) since July 24, 2026. On a 20-tonne lot worth $20,000 that is $280 + $2,500 = $2,780. Brown jasmine (1006.20.40.25) is 2.1¢/kg plus 12.5%. Thailand shipped $966M of rice to the U.S. in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for rice?
faqs.answer: Heading 1006. Paddy rice is 1006.10, husked (brown) rice 1006.20, semi-milled or wholly milled rice 1006.30 and broken rice 1006.40. The 10-digit U.S. lines split milled rice into jasmine (1006.30.90.57), basmati (1006.30.90.59), other long grain, medium grain, short grain and parboiled (1006.30.10, 11.2%). Rice flour is in Chapter 11, not here.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for wheat?
faqs.answer: Heading 1001. Durum wheat is 1001.11 (seed, 0.65¢/kg) and 1001.19 (other, 0.65¢/kg); other wheat and meslin is 1001.91 (seed, 2.8%) and 1001.99 (other, 0.35¢/kg). Wheat flour is 1101 in Chapter 11, not here.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for corn and popcorn kernels?
faqs.answer: Heading 1005. Seed corn is 1005.10 (Free, only with the foreign government's certified seed tags); yellow dent corn 1005.90.20 (0.05¢/kg); popcorn kernels 1005.90.40.40 and other corn 1005.90.40.60 (0.25¢/kg). Sweet corn is in Chapter 7, and corn flour and corn starch are in Chapter 11.

faqs.question: Are there U.S. tariffs on wheat and oats from Canada?
faqs.answer: Not if they qualify for USMCA. Oats are Free at base and most wheat is 0.35¢/kg, which USMCA makes Free, and USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt from the 10% Section 301 duty on Canadian products (9903.05.93). Grain that doesn't qualify pays the base rate plus 10% of value (9903.05.29). The 35% IEEPA duty of 2025 ended on February 24, 2026. Canada shipped $693M of wheat and $344M of oats to the U.S. in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the tariff code for quinoa?
faqs.answer: 1008.50.00, split into certified organic (1008.50.00.10) and other (1008.50.00.90). The general rate is 1.1%. Peruvian quinoa is Free at base with a Peru TPA claim but still pays the 12.5% Section 301 duty (9903.05.63); Bolivian quinoa pays only the 1.1% base rate, because Bolivia is not one of the 60 Section 301 economies.

faqs.question: What do I need to import rice into the U.S.?
searchedAs: how to import rice from india to usa
can i bring rice to usa
faqs.answer: For commercial rice: FDA prior notice before arrival (21 CFR 1.279), a registered foreign facility (21 CFR 1.225) and an importer with a Foreign Supplier Verification Program (21 CFR 1.502). Rice from khapra-beetle countries such as India and Pakistan needs a phytosanitary certificate stating it was inspected and found free of khapra beetle, and rice from those countries may not be brought in passenger baggage (7 CFR 319.75-2). Paddy rice is restricted as seed.

faqs.question: How much rice does the U.S. import, and from where?
searchedAs: how much rice is imported to us
is rice imported into the us
faqs.answer: $1.64B of rice in 2025, about half of all U.S. cereal imports. Thailand supplied $966M, India $401M, Pakistan $50M, Argentina $38M, Vietnam $31M and China $30M. Milled rice (1006.30) was $1.56B of the total.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import corn from?
faqs.answer: $245M of corn in 2025: Canada $83M, Argentina $64M, Chile $39M, Türkiye $24.5M, Brazil $11.7M and Mexico $7.5M. $75M of it was seed corn (1005.10), down from $118M in 2024.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for wild rice?
faqs.answer: 1008.90.01.20 (other cereals, wild rice), with a general rate of 1.1%. Wild rice is classified with the other cereals in 1008.90, not with rice in heading 1006.
